label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Peter, your nine years in payroll count for something here. The risk of people becoming dependent on advances is real, as is the problem of recovering money when someone leaves. I also agree that an informal arrangement where HR hears everyone’s story and makes a judgement call is not a good system.

Where I disagree, quite strongly, is with “it’s painful for one or two pay cycles and then people adjust”. We tried closing the window in 2025, on almost exactly the grounds you’ve set out. We had to reverse the decision.

For context, we have about 340 staff, with depots in Embakasi and Changamwe in Mombasa. Mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. Different business from Brenda’s, but I suspect some similar household pressures.

We stopped advances in February 2025 after pushback from Finance. We gave two months’ notice, rather than your suggested three, and held a financial literacy session with the SACCO. So we did not follow your proposal to the letter, but we tried the same basic approach: explain the change, give people time, offer an alternative and stop lending.

What followed was not simply a difficult couple of pay cycles.

In the six months after closure, debt collector and loan-app calls to the office went from a handful to **61 calls logged by reception**. Some apps were calling supervisors whom employees had listed as “referees”.

I’m not saying those were 61 separate borrowers, or that every call was caused by our decision. But they were 61 calls our reception had to deal with, alongside supervisors being pulled into employees’ borrowing problems. The loan contracts may have been private; the consequences were arriving at work.

We also saw an increase in unplanned absence on the two days after month-end. Our Fleet Manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers being away “sorting out” loans. That is his operational assessment, not proof that stopping advances caused every absence. Still, it was enough to make us question whether we had actually saved the business money.

The cost of an advance was visible in payroll. The time spent fielding collection calls, following up absence and dealing with missed runs was scattered across reception, HR, supervisors and fleet operations. Closing one budget line did not make those costs disappear.

One case particularly changed my view. A loader at Changamwe had six loan apps going at once by the time he came to me, borrowing from one to pay another. It took us four months working with payroll to unwind the situation. That was considerably more HR work than processing a controlled advance would have been.

On SACCOs, I agree they should be part of the answer. But ours takes two to three weeks to process a loan and requires guarantors. That may work for a planned expense. It does not solve the problem of a child being sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday.

Financial literacy is useful too. We should keep doing it. But on KES 28,000 a month, there is a limit to how much emergency capacity someone can create through better budgeting. Some requests will reflect poor planning; others reflect very little room between income and essential expenses. We need a system that recognises both, rather than assuming every emergency is a lesson the employee has failed to learn.

We reopened advances in September 2025, but we did **not** reopen the old informal scheme.

The written policy now provides for:

- A maximum advance of **40% of net pay**.
- One advance per pay cycle.
- Full repayment at the next payroll.
- No fee.
- Requests through the payroll portal, rather than a queue outside my office.
- A check on existing deductions before approval.

That last point matters. We check the Employment Act’s limit on total deductions of two-thirds of wages before approving anything. The 40% cap is not an automatic entitlement regardless of what someone already owes. An application can be within our headline cap and still fail the deduction check. Nobody should reach month-end and discover there is nothing left.

Since reopening, we have been handling roughly 55–70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. Recovery has been 100% apart from two leavers, with roughly KES 14,000 written off for the year.

I would not dismiss that loss, and it supports your point that leavers are a genuine risk. Nor would I claim our administration costs are zero. But those are actual figures we can put against the alternative, rather than assuming that refusing advances leaves the employer with no cost or exposure.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. What changed his mind was that the forecast impact is known in advance. There is a fixed ceiling and a defined repayment point, rather than an open-ended collection of promises coming out of HR.

You are also right that someone requesting an advance every month deserves attention. An advance moves payday; it does not increase salary. We should not pretend otherwise. But regular use is something to monitor and discuss privately, not necessarily a reason to remove the facility from everyone. Otherwise the employee who has one genuine emergency loses access because another employee is struggling every month.

Brenda, for your meeting on the 18th, I would separate two questions: should the current informal arrangement continue, and should advances be abolished altogether? You can agree with Finance that the first is not acceptable without agreeing to the second.

I would go in with whatever numbers you can pull together before then: how many advances you issue each month, their total value, how many are repeat requests, what has actually been lost on leavers and how much staff time administration takes. If some of that information is missing, say so. Our figures are an example of what happened elsewhere, not a forecast of what will happen at your firm.

Then propose a written, time-limited trial with a review date. A 40% net-pay cap, once per pay cycle, repayment at the next payroll and a single documented application route would give you a concrete starting point. Agree who approves requests, who checks deductions and how Finance sees the expected cash requirement. Track repeat use, recovery, exceptions and administration time during the trial.

I would also ask that the review consider absence, collection calls and operational disruption, not just the amount advanced. Those costs are harder to gather because different departments carry them, but they still belong in the discussion.

Peter, I think we agree that HR should not run an informal lending desk. Our experience was that shutting it down entirely did not get us out of employees’ financial problems. We ended up spending time on more difficult problems, with less control over them.

For us, written rules and limits have worked better than either an open door or a completely closed one. That is the option I would want Brenda to have properly considered on the 18th.
